text:
The flat was always on the third floor, and it was always his. This was the first thing Daniel knew in the dream: that he had paid for it, every month, for years, and had not once come to look at it. He would climb a stairwell that smelled of radiators and floor polish, a key already in his hand, feeling the specific shame of a man who has let something go to waste. The door opened onto a long hallway with more rooms than the building could possibly have contained. Some were empty and bright. One had a bath in it, and nothing else. In the last, Rachel would be standing at the window with her back to him, watering a plant or folding a tea towel, and she would say, without turning, "You came."

That was all. She never said anything unkind. Daniel would wake at ten past four with his heart going as though he had been caught at something, and lie listening to Isabel breathe, and feel the flat recede down its corridor.

He had been having the dream, on and off, since February. It was now the end of May. He had not mentioned it to anyone, partly because it seemed too stupid, and partly because he knew what Isabel would say, or thought he did. Isabel was a speech therapist, and she had a way of tilting her head when you said something revealing, as though checking it for a lisp.

He told her on a Sunday, over the wreckage of a late breakfast. She was reading the paper with her feet in his lap, and he said, to the back of the Review section, "I keep dreaming about Rachel."

The paper came down an inch. "Rachel Rachel?"

"There's only the one."

"There might be others you haven't told me about." She folded the paper. Her face was not alarmed, which he was grateful for; it was merely attentive. "What happens?"

He described the stairwell, the key, the rooms. He found he was embarrassed by the bath. "It's not even a nice bath. It's one of those avocado ones from the seventies."

"And Rachel's just there."

"Watering something."

"Does she look happy?"

He considered. In the dream Rachel looked as she had at thirty-four, the age she had been when he last saw her as his wife, in the kitchen of the house in Walthamstow, holding a mug she then put down very carefully, the way you put down something you intend to leave. "She looks like she's waiting," he said. "Not for me, exactly. Just waiting."

Isabel nodded slowly. She moved her feet off his lap and sat up, and he understood he had said a more serious thing than he had meant to. "Do you want to see her?"

"No. God, no. I think I just feel I owe her something. Or the flat does. The flat is the thing I owe."

"That's a very odd sentence," Isabel said, kindly, and got up to make more coffee.

They did not discuss it again that day, but it sat in the house with them, a third person who had come for lunch and not left. Isabel was nearly fifty and had been married once, briefly, to a man named Tobias who now lived in Lisbon and sent her a card every Christmas with a photograph of a different dog. That evening, as they washed up, she said, "We never had a single row, Tobias and I. Then one day he said he'd been unhappy for three years, and I said, 'Why didn't you tell me?' and he said, 'You'd have been so reasonable about it.'" She laughed, but not very much. "I've never forgiven him. It was true."

Daniel dried the plate for longer than it needed. He and Rachel had rowed constantly, magnificently, over small things, and it had turned out to be no protection at all. He said so, and Isabel said perhaps there was no protection, perhaps that was the whole difficulty, and they stood in the yellow light of the kitchen, holding the quiet between them like a dish neither wanted to put away.

Over the next week Isabel became careful with him, and he with her, so that their evenings took on the tone of two people carrying a ladder through a narrow house. She asked about the dream once more, on Wednesday, and he said it had not come back, which was true, and felt oddly like a lie.

On Saturday he went looking for a fuse. The hall light had gone. At the back of the drawer in the hall table, under a takeaway menu and a tape measure, he found a ring of keys he did not recognize.

There were four, dull and slightly furred with age. Two were Yale-type; one was long and brass, the sort that opens a door in a film about a castle; the fourth was tiny, for a padlock. A paper tag was threaded through the ring, and on it, in blue biro faded to the color of a vein, was written *Boathouse — Hereford*, in Rachel's handwriting.

He sat down on the stairs.

It came back not as a memory but as a temperature. It was August, the year before they married, and Rachel's uncle Gordon, who had a bad hip and a worse temper, had lent them the key to a shed on the Wye where he kept a green Canadian canoe. He remembered the weight of the boat on his shoulders, the smell of river mud and old rope, Rachel in front of him in a man's sweater with the sleeves pushed up, shouting directions he ignored. They had capsized, in the end, in water so shallow it was less a catastrophe than an indignity, and had sat in the shallows laughing until they were cold, and then eaten warm sausage rolls in the car with the heater on high. It was possibly the happiest day of his life. He had carried the keys through three moves without once asking what they opened.

He understood then something about the flat. It was not that he owed Rachel anything. It was that somewhere in him was a set of rooms he had paid for and never visited: the man who had capsized in the Wye, who was pleased by sausage rolls, who did not tilt his head at his own feelings. Rachel was simply the one standing in the last room, because she had been there when he last used it.

Isabel came home from the market with a bag of apricots and found him still on the stairs.

"The fuse," she said.

"I haven't done the fuse." He held up the keys. "They're to a boathouse. Rachel's uncle's. We used to borrow a canoe."

She put down the bag. She did not tilt her head, which he noticed, and loved her for. She sat beside him and took the ring, turning the tag to the light. "That's her writing?"

"Yes."

"It's a nice hand." She said this in a perfectly neutral voice, then added, "I'm not going to pretend I don't mind a little. Is that all right?"

"It's more than all right." He looked at her. "It was a wonderful day, Isabel. I'd forgotten. I'd put the whole of that time in the box marked *Didn't Work*, and never went back to check what else was in there. I think the dream was that. A box I hadn't opened."

"Well," she said, "you've opened it now." She gave him back the keys, smiling, though carefully. "Does the boathouse still exist?"

"God, no. Gordon died years ago. It's probably been turned into a flat." He heard what he had said and laughed, and after a moment she did too, helplessly, until she had to put her head on his shoulder.

"I've never been in a canoe," she said, when she had recovered. "I get seasick in a pedalo."

"I steer by guessing."

"Then we'll be well matched."

They went the following Saturday, not to the Wye but to a hire place on the Thames above Oxford, where a boy with a sunburned neck gave them a bright red boat and a laminated card of instructions that Isabel read aloud, with feeling, as they wobbled out from the bank. She sat in front. She paddled on the wrong side, then the right, then, in a moment of improvisation, both. Daniel, behind her, watched the back of her neck, where her hair had come loose, and the small, serious set of her shoulders as she tried to learn something at nearly fifty, in public, with no one to be reasonable for.

"Left," he said. "No, your left."

"This is my left."

"That's very definitely your right."

"Oh, for heaven's sake." She turned around, laughing, nearly taking them over, and they both grabbed the gunwales and held there, rocking, while a pair of swans regarded them with a contempt so total it was almost courteous.

The keys were in his pocket. Somewhere under the water, he thought, there might be a bath, an avocado one, and a corridor of lit rooms, and a woman at a window who had finished watering the plant and gone home. He felt no pull toward it. He felt the boat settling beneath him, the wet blade of the paddle in his hands, and Isabel's back, warm and upright and a little crooked, going on ahead.

"Are we doing all right?" she called, without turning.

"We're going in a circle," he said.

"Is that bad?"

"I think it's the only way anyone gets anywhere," said Daniel, and dug in, and the red boat, after some consideration, began to move.
